Michigan Tribal Casinos Withhold Revenue-Sharing Payments

Published September 30, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Payments Michigan's tribal casinos share with the state have plunged 71% since 2022, and the decline is accelerating as more tribes join a dispute over whether the state's gambling expansion broke the exclusivity promises in their casino compacts, according to reporting this week from Crain's Detroit Business, relayed by Casino.org and CDC Gaming.

What's happening

Tribal casino revenue-sharing payments to Michigan fell from $52.8 million in 2022 to $15.4 million in 2025. The Pokagon Band, which still shared $11.7 million in 2025, became the latest tribe to join the group withholding payments as of September 28, 2026. The Nottawaseppi Huron Band, which contributed $18.5 million in 2024, stopped paying in February 2026. That leaves the Hannahville Indian Community as the only tribe still paying in full, contributing roughly $644,000 in 2025 — a fraction of what the program once generated. Michigan's tribes have paid more than $1.1 billion in revenue-sharing since the program began, while tribal and commercial operators together paid $624.6 million in state taxes on online gaming in 2025 alone.

The tribes argue that Michigan's expansion of gambling access — including online lottery games introduced in 2014 and the 2019 legalization of online casinos and sports betting — violated exclusivity protections built into their compacts, which were meant to shield tribal casinos from state-sanctioned competition in exchange for the revenue-sharing payments. Little River Band was the first to stop paying, in 2023, followed by Gun Lake Tribe in 2025.

Why it matters

The lost revenue is landing directly on the Michigan Economic Development Corporation, which relies on the payments to fund the Michigan Strategic Fund and has already disclosed layoffs this month as it faces both the funding shortfall and separate legislative cuts to its state appropriations. The dispute leaves Michigan facing a structural funding problem tied directly to how it regulates online gambling, with no resolution in sight until the underlying compacts come up for potential renegotiation between 2028 and 2030. For the broader industry, the standoff is a concrete example of the tension that online gambling expansion can create with tribal gaming exclusivity agreements, a dynamic playing out in other states as more of them legalize online casino products.

Sources

  • Casino.org — "Michigan Tribal Casino Payments Plunge 71% as Gambling Expansion Tests Exclusivity Deals"
  • CDC Gaming — "Michigan's Tribal Casino Payments Plunge, Creating Funding Problem for Economic Development Agency"
